summary: Introduces content networks and content internetworking, the interconnection of content networks sometimes called CDN peering, and defines a shared vocabulary for discussing them. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 7336.

eli5.summary: Companies that deliver web content faster use their own networks, and sometimes they want to work together. This note gives everyone the same words to talk about that. It was later replaced by RFC 7336.

questions: what is a content delivery network
subtitle: A vocabulary for understanding how content delivery networks interconnect and share resources.

tldr.problem: Content networks (CDNs) solve the problem of delivering large files quickly by replicating content across multiple locations, but when different CDNs want to share or peer with each other, they lack common terminology and concepts.
tldr.mechanism: Defines a shared vocabulary for content networks, including roles (origin server, surrogate, user agent), functions (request-routing, distribution, accounting), and operations, then extends it to describe how networks interconnect through gateways and negotiated relationships.
tldr.outcome: The vocabulary enables CDI (Content Distribution Internetworking), allowing independent CDNs to interconnect while hiding internal details from each other. RFC 7336 later refined these concepts further.

today: RFC 7336 replaced this RFC with an updated model that builds on these foundations. The vocabulary defined here remains the basis for discussing CDN interconnection.

sections.title: The Content Distribution Problem
sections.content:
Content networks are built to solve the problem of delivering files to large numbers of users quickly. Sending every request to a single origin server would create bottlenecks and network congestion. Instead, content is replicated to servers closer to users.

This RFC builds on existing taxonomy from RFC 3040 (web caching) and introduces consistent terminology for discussing how content networks work and how they connect to each other. The document avoids vague terms like cache in favor of more precise terms like caching proxy or surrogate.
sections.eli5: When websites get popular, sending every request to the original server is too slow. Companies copy the content to many locations so users get it faster. This RFC teaches the words used to talk about these systems.

sections.title: Types of Content Networks
sections.content:
The RFC describes three main approaches. Caching proxies are placed near users, and users send all requests through them. When a cache misses, it fetches the content from the origin or a parent cache. Server farms place multiple origin servers near each other behind a load-balancing switch that distributes requests across them. Content delivery networks (CDNs) combine elements of both: they deploy replica servers (surrogates) in geographically diverse locations, use a request-routing system to direct users to a nearby surrogate, and have distribution infrastructure to push content from the origin to surrogates.

CDNs add a critical capability: they direct a user's request to a good replica based on dynamic information about network conditions and surrogate load, not just static geography. A CDN typically includes request-routing infrastructure, surrogate servers, distribution systems, and accounting systems for billing.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to speed up content delivery. One: sit between the user and the origin and remember things. Two: put multiple copies of the origin behind a smart switch. Three: put copies all over the world and send each user to the nearest one, which is a CDN.

sections.title: The CDI Vocabulary
sections.content:
A publisher controls content and partners with a CDN operator. An origin is where the authoritative copy lives. A surrogate is a replica server that delivers content on behalf of the origin. A user agent is the browser or client that initiates requests. Request-routing steers a user to a suitable surrogate. Distribution moves content from the origin to surrogates. Delivery is the actual serving of content from a surrogate to a user agent. Accounting measures and records what happened, often for billing.

For interconnection, a Content Internetworking Gateway (CIG) is the point of contact between two networks. An originating network requests services from an enlisted network via a negotiated relationship. Content advertisements describe what content is available on a network, while distribution advertisements describe the capabilities of surrogates.
sections.eli5: The origin holds the master copy. Surrogates are copies. The request-router decides which surrogate to use. Distribution moves stuff to the surrogates. Delivery gives it to the user. When two CDNs team up, they make an agreement and use a gateway to talk to each other.

sections.title: Why CDNs Interconnect
sections.content:
No single CDN can achieve infinite scale or reach. Interconnecting CDNs allows them to share surrogates and distribution capacity, improving both scale (total infrastructure size) and reach (geographic diversity). This requires common protocols and understanding of what each network is offering.

The RFC notes that content internetworking happens via distribution internetworking (exchanging content between networks), request-routing internetworking (sharing the ability to direct requests to additional surrogates), and accounting internetworking (exchanging billing data). The scope and form depend on the negotiated business relationship.
sections.eli5: One CDN might be great at Asia but weak in Europe. Another is strong in Europe but weak in Asia. By connecting them, both get better coverage and share the cost of servers.
